report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is plausible but not established: observational research links higher *chocolate* intake with lower stroke incidence, but it does not prove that eating dark chocolate prevents stroke.

A 2012 meta-analysis of five prospective studies (4,260 stroke cases) found that people in the highest chocolate-intake category had a 19% lower relative stroke risk than those in the lowest category (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.73–0.90). These studies are susceptible to residual confounding: chocolate eaters may differ in diet, activity, income, health status, or other behaviors. Importantly, they generally assessed chocolate overall, not specifically dark chocolate.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22933736/

Evidence is also inconsistent. In the large Women’s Health Initiative observational cohort, chocolate consumption was **not** associated with stroke risk.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6862600/

There is a credible mechanism: cocoa flavanols can modestly improve blood pressure and vascular measures. But the Cochrane review found no long-term randomized trials of cocoa products measuring clinical outcomes such as stroke or heart attack. Thus, improving a risk marker is not proof of stroke prevention.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6478304/

Regulators likewise remain cautious. FDA permits only a qualified claim for *high-flavanol* cocoa products, explicitly noting that the evidence supporting a reduced cardiovascular-disease risk is “very limited”; this is not a stroke-prevention claim and does not apply to ordinary dark chocolate generally.  
https://www.fda.gov/food/hfp-constituent-updates/fda-announces-qualified-health-claim-cocoa-flavanols-high-flavanol-cocoa-powder-and-reduced-risk

**Practical takeaway:** Dark chocolate can be an occasional food, preferably high-cocoa and low in added sugar, but should not be relied upon to lower stroke risk. Established prevention—blood-pressure control, not smoking, exercise, and an overall healthy diet—has much stronger evidence.
